The Anglican Communion is constituted by the set of Episcopal Churches that belong to the Anglican confession and derives from the extension of the Church of England to other countries. In Spain the Anglican Communion is formed by two episcopal jurisdictions: the Spanish Reformed Episcopal Church 3 (hereinafter, IERE) and the Spanish Section of the Diocese in Europe of the Church of England 4 (also called the Diocese of Gibraltar in Europe). Both jurisdictions are integrated into FEREDE 5.

1 Work published in GARCÍA GARCÍA, R., GONZÁLEZ SÁNCHEZ, M. (Eds.), 
Application and development of the Agreement between the Spanish State and FEREDE, Fundación 
Universitaria Española, Madrid, 2008, pp. 169-188. (ISBN: 978-84-7392-700-0) 
2 I wish to thank D. Carlos López Lozano, Diocesan Bishop of the Spanish Reformed Episcopal Church and Assistant Bishop of the Diocese 
of Gibraltar in Europe, for the help provided in preparing this article. For more information on the subject, see: S. NEILL, Anglicanism, Madrid, 
1986; F. SERRANO ÁLVAREZ, Against Wind and Tide, Terrassa, 2000, and C. LÓPEZ LOZANO, Precedents 
of the I.E.R.E., Madrid, 1991. 
3 It was founded in Gibraltar in 1868 and was reorganized in diocesan form in Seville in 
1880. This foundation arose from a Synod in which the episcopal form of government was adopted. 
It is currently a Member of the Anglican Communion and of the World Council of Churches and belongs to the 
KEK Conference of Churches and to the Conference of Latin Protestant Churches of Southern Europe 
(CEPPLE). 
4 Its origins date from 1605. Thanks to the ratification of the Treaty of London signed by 
James I of England and Philip III of Spain, English residents in Spain were authorized to celebrate 
private worship (in their homes). In 1842 a jurisdiction was created that supervised Anglican chaplaincies 
in Spanish territory, and in 1988 the Diocese in Europe of the Church of 
England was established (to which the Anglican chaplaincies established in Spain belong).  
5 See Structure and composition of the Federation of Evangelical Religious Entities of 
Spain, in Cuadernos de Información, 1-2, 2007, p. 11. 
In Spain, the Anglican Communion has about 39 parishes and chaplaincies, 
with about a hundred places of worship 6 and a membership of about 200,000 people 7 who 
participate actively in the life of the Church. 
In the IERE, worship is celebrated according to the ancient Hispanic Liturgy, 
also known as Visigothic or Mozarabic. The so-called Mozarabic, Visigothic, or 
Hispanic rite is the liturgy of the ancient Spanish Church that was consolidated around the 
sixth century on the Iberian Peninsula, in the Visigothic Kingdom of Toledo, and that was practiced in the 
Hispanic territories until the eleventh century (both in areas under Christian and 
Muslim rule) 8. Later it was preserved only in the city of Toledo, under rather 
precarious conditions. The Mozarabic liturgy has been maintained and celebrated without interruption in Spain 
mainly thanks to the Mozarabic Community of Toledo and the efforts, 
chiefly, of Cardinals Cisneros and Lorenzana. In the mid-nineteenth century the 
IERE, on the initiative of its First Bishop, also began to use for its worship the 
ancient Hispanic liturgy.

2. The concept of marriage in the Anglican Communion 
The life of the Church is governed by the provisions of what is established in the 
Book of Bases and Canons of the IERE 9, which was approved at the XXXVI Synod 10  
and ratified at the XLI Synod 11 and in the spirit of the "Chicago-Lambeth Quadrilateral" 12  
approved by the Lambeth Conference of 1888. This document affirms the 
essential elements of faith and order for achieving unity among Christians. 
Among the canons, canon 11 concerns marriage. It is precisely the one that 
gives us the definition of marriage 13 when it says: “... holy marriage, 
contracted within the community of faith, is the physical and spiritual union of a man and 
a woman, with mutual consent and with the intention that it be for life.”

6 These figures do not coincide with those offered by the Registry of Religious Entities, since 
notification of the opening of a place of worship to the Registry is not obligatory, but optional. 
7 Many of them are retirees from the United Kingdom who have fixed their residence in Spain. This 
explains why the number of marriages celebrated in Anglican form in Spain is not very high, 
since they number around 30 marriages a year. According to data provided by the IERE, in 
2007 it was known that 28 marriages had been celebrated (but as of February 28, 
2008, the statistics were not yet finalized); in 2006, 22 marriages were contracted in Anglican religious form; 
and in 2005, there were 31. 
8 http://www.anglicanos.org/ (consulted March 8, 2007). 
9 Technically they are the Fundamental Bases of denomination, doctrine, personality, government, 
and discipline of the IERE. These Bases were drafted in accordance with the general doctrines of the Anglican Communion 
throughout the world and, once approved, were made known to the Archbishop of 
Canterbury. 
10 It was held on June 10 and 11, 1982. 
11 It was held between June 4 and 6, 1993. 
12 Four things are defined as essential for unity in the Anglican Church, namely: 
a) The Scriptures of the Old and New Testament. 
b) The ecumenical creeds (Apostles' and Nicene). 
c) The Sacraments of Jesus Christ. 
d) The Historic Episcopate. 
13 Canon 11.2.c). 
This definition deserves to be analyzed in detail and, for that reason, we have thought it 
appropriate to dissect it into four parts: 
1st. Holy marriage, contracted within the community of faith. 
Anglicans, members of FEREDE, have the particularity 14 of the 
existence of the Sacraments 15. For them there are two Sacraments: Baptism 16 and the 
Eucharist 17. And five sacramental rites 18: Confirmation 19, Penance 20, 
Marriage, Anointing of the sick 21, and Holy Orders 22. 
Therefore, marriage celebrated in Anglican religious form is a sacramental 
rite. Even 23 when only one of the two spouses is baptized 
Anglican.

14 Like the Roman Catholic Apostolic Church.  
15 Inasmuch as they are actions of Christ and of the Church, they are signs and means by which 
faith is expressed and strengthened, worship is rendered to God, and the sanctification of humankind is carried out, and therefore 
they contribute in great measure to creating, confirming, and manifesting ecclesiastical communion (canon 840 of the 
Code of Canon Law). The Council of Trent solemnly established that there are seven Sacraments 
of the New Law, namely: Baptism, Confirmation, Holy Eucharist, Penance, Extreme Unction, Orders, 
and Marriage. The same enumeration had already been made in the Decree for the Armenians of the Council of 
Florence (1439); in the Profession of Faith of Michael Palaeologus, offered by Gregory X at the Council of 
Lyon (1274); and at the council held in London in 1237. And in the Westminster Confession of Faith, of 
1647, we can read that: "The sacraments ordained by God are not only badges or tokens of the 
Christian man's profession, but rather sure witnesses and effectual signs of grace and of 
God's good will toward us, by which He works invisibly in us and not only 
quickens but also strengthens and confirms our faith in Him" (Chapter XXVII.1). 
16 For Anglicans, Baptism is the doorway into the family of God. It is administered 
once only to each person (generally in childhood). It is performed with water, symbolizing the cleansing of 
sin, and the Most Holy Trinity is invoked. The inward and spiritual gift is union with Christ in his 
death and resurrection, the forgiveness of sins, and a new birth into the family of God: the Church. 
17 It is the commemoration and thanksgiving for the death and resurrection of Christ. 
Bread and wine are used. The body of Christ is given, taken, and eaten in a heavenly and spiritual manner, and 
the means by which it is received and eaten is faith. Through the sacrament of the Eucharist, the members of the 
Church offer themselves to God in repentance, love, and faith, remember his death, testify to his 
sacrifice, and renew their hope in the heavenly meal. The IERE practices a policy of open 
communion toward communicant members of other Christian churches. 
18 The sacramental rites also have sacramental value, since participation in them 
communicates divine grace; but, in the words of Mortimer, “they are not necessary for salvation in the same 
way as the other two sacraments, since they are not necessary for all.” Some also call them 
“the five lesser Sacraments.” 
19 Anglicans understand confirmation as the service by which, through prayer and 
the laying on of hands by the bishop, and with the action of the Holy Spirit, the 
commitment to Christ made in baptism is renewed and strengthened. 
20 Penance is the acknowledgment and confession to God of sins, made freely and 
voluntarily in the presence of a minister, and with a sincere desire to change one's attitude. Through 
absolution, the minister affirms God's forgiveness and the reconciliation of the sinner. 
21 Anointing of the sick is the service by which God's grace is given for physical and spiritual 
healing in response to faith and prayer. It is shown by the laying on of hands or by anointing 
with oil. 
22 Through this rite, Christians are consecrated to the service of God. They receive the power and grace that 
helps them dedicate their lives to the good of the community by teaching, administering the sacraments, and 
governing the Church. 
23 Unlike what is established by Canon Law, which in canon 1055.1 states: “The 
matrimonial covenant… was raised by Christ the Lord to the dignity of a sacrament between the baptized”; and in 
its number 2 establishes: “Therefore, between the baptized, there can be no valid matrimonial contract that is not 
In principle, Anglicans are obliged to celebrate their marriage 
in religious form. Also when only one of the two spouses is 
baptized 24. And, if this situation arises, the unbaptized party is not required to make 
an express declaration committing not to impede the baptized party 
from continuing to participate actively in the life of the Church 25.  
Despite what has been said regarding the obligation to celebrate 
marriage in Anglican religious form, if the spouses decide to marry 
only in civil form, the Church recognizes the existence of that matrimonial bond. 
Moreover, it continues to allow the spouses to participate actively in the life of the 
community. This is probably due to recognition of the human value of their 
civil marriage 26. 
2nd It is the physical 27 and spiritual union of a man and a woman. 
It is a clear expression of the non-acceptance of homosexual marriage, as 
marriage. 
In this sense, the Permanent Commission of FEREDE issued a declaration 
on the effects for the Churches of FEREDE of the modification of the Civil Code in 
matters of marriage 28, which read as follows: 
“After the approval of Law 13/2005 modifying the Civil Code in 
matters of marriage, the Plenary Commission after due deliberation 
agrees: 
a. To ratify that, in marriage celebrated according to the evangelical rite, under 
the Cooperation Agreements, the spouses must be a man and a woman. 
b. That certifications for the celebration of marriages by the 
evangelical rite shall not be issued when the spouses are persons of the same sex.

be a sacrament.” Thus, marriage between two baptized persons, if it is a valid marriage, is always 
a sacrament. And if one of the spouses is unbaptized, it cannot be a sacramental marriage.  
24 Canon 11.2.d). 
25 This practice stands out as different from that of the Roman Catholic Apostolic Church, which 
establishes in its canon 1125, 1º and 2º: “If there is a just and reasonable cause, the local Ordinary may 
grant this permission; but he must not grant it unless the following conditions are fulfilled: 1º that the 
Catholic party declare that they are prepared to remove dangers of defecting from the faith, and sincerely promise 
to do all in their power to have all the offspring baptized and brought up in the Catholic 
Church; 2º that the other party be informed at an appropriate time of the promises which the Catholic party 
is to make, so that it is certain that the non-Catholic party is truly aware of the promise and of the obligation of the 
Catholic party.” 
26 In this sense, see M.F. POMPEDDA, Fede e Sacramento del matrimonio. Mancanza di 
Fede e consenso matrimoniale: aspetti giuridici, in Quaderni, Studio Rotale, II, Rome, 1987, pp. 41-71. 
27 Procreation is not one of the essential purposes of marriage. Sexuality is 
understood as a gift of God. This contrasts with what is established in canon 1055.1 of the Code of 
Canon Law: “The matrimonial covenant, by which a man and a woman establish between themselves a 
partnership of the whole of life, is by its nature ordered toward the good of the spouses and the 
procreation and education of offspring…”; and in canon 1096.1: “For matrimonial consent 
to exist, it is necessary that the contracting parties at least not be ignorant that marriage is a permanent 
partnership between a man and a woman ordered to the procreation of offspring…”. 
28 This declaration arose from the meeting of the Permanent Commission of FEREDE held on 
October 11, 2005. 
c. That ministers of worship who, in fulfillment of what is set out above, 
intend to celebrate or do celebrate marriages between two persons of the same 
sex, by the evangelical rite and under the Cooperation Agreements, shall be 
automatically deprived of the conformity of the Permanent Commission of 
FEREDE. Therefore, as established by article 3 of Law 24/1992, they cease to be 
considered ministers of worship for the purposes of the said law. 
d. That Churches or ministers of worship who breach these agreements shall be 
subject to proceedings that will be referred to the Plenary Commission or 
Permanent Commission so that they may decide what they consider appropriate.” 
From this we can note that: 
1. At the time of the approval of the Cooperation Agreement concluded between the 
Spanish State and FEREDE 29, the provisions of article 7 were 
conceived only for marriages celebrated between a man and a woman 
(for that was also the only option for marriage contracted in civil form). By 
contrast, today, even though it is possible to contract civil marriage between two 
persons of the same sex, the Churches belonging to FEREDE indicate 
expressly that for marriages celebrated in their religious form, the 
requirement that the spouses be of different sex continues to apply. 
2. This interpretation is possible because of the separation existing between the Spanish 
State and the various religious confessions. Hence the modification made in the 
Civil Code affects only civil marriages, insofar as the religious 
confessions position themselves against the adoption of these postulates. 
3rd. With mutual consent. 
This means that the parties must have sufficient capacity to understand what 
marriage is 30, and that consent must be manifested in a 
completely free manner 31. 
4th. With the intention that it be for life. 
This means that marriage is conceived as indissoluble, and to that end, 
Anglicans have, in principle, no mechanism for dissolving the matrimonial bond. 
Nevertheless, this statement must be qualified on the basis of: 
a) A civil avenue: the effect of civil divorce is recognized. Although divorce 32 
is considered a grave error in Anglican practice and “a priori” the divorced are not permitted 
to contract a new marriage 33.

29 By Law 24/1992, of November 10 (published in the BOE of November 12, 
1992).  
30 Canon 11.2.c). 
31 This freedom must be both internal and external. That is, there can be no conditioning 
of any kind at the moment of the external manifestation of consent. Precisely at this 
point we see the concordance between what is required by Canon Law—which in its canon 1103 says: “Marriage 
contracted by violence or by grave fear is invalid…”—and what is required by the Anglican Communion. 
This is logical, since the freedom with which marriage must be contracted is a requirement of 
natural law. 
b) An ecclesiastical avenue: following what is provided in Doctrinal Base Six 34, the 
General Synod of the Church 35, as the highest authority over the faithful, 
could pronounce itself regarding the dissolution of a flagrant case of failure of a 
marriage. 
And there would even be a third avenue (also ecclesiastical) corresponding to the 
Roman Catholic Apostolic Church: those cases in which a 
non-Catholic party seeks to challenge their marriage before an ecclesiastical judge—even 
while the challenging party remains non-Catholic—in order to contract a canonical marriage 
with a Catholic person 36. It would even be possible that the canonical legislator had 
taken into account the fact that many Christian Churches and communities lack 
a proper matrimonial judicial system and, therefore, no foreign territory would be being invaded 37.

For a marriage contracted in Anglican religious form to have 
civil validity, it is required: a) that there be true matrimonial consent; and b) that there be 
no legal impediments. 
a) True matrimonial consent. 
Article 45 of the Civil Code states: “There is no marriage without matrimonial 
consent. Any condition, term, or mode of the consent shall be deemed not 
written.” 
b) That there be no legal impediments. 
These are those established in articles 46 and 47 of the Civil Code: 
1. Minority of age without emancipation.

32 Divorce does not cause one to fall into excommunication. 
33 To avoid falling into the same error again. But, extraordinarily, a new marriage is permitted 
provided that the divorced person interested in remarrying 
had not been the cause of the divorce for reasons of adultery or infidelity, unless they demonstrate 
that they have resolved the problem that caused their first marital failure. 
34 Chapter II of the Bases, dedicated to the general organization of the Church. 
35 It is subject to the authority of Christ. 
36 In this regard, one must recall canon 1674, 1º: “Those competent to challenge 
marriage are: 1º the spouses…”; canon 1476: “Any person, whether baptized or not, may sue 
in court; and the party lawfully sued has the obligation to respond”; and the Decree of the 
Apostolic Signatura of May 28, 1993 addressed to the Apostolic Vicariate of Sweden: “The Catholic 
Church enjoys jurisdiction to determine the nullity or otherwise of marriage contracted between non-
Catholics, if one of them seeks to contract a new marriage with a Catholic party,” in JC, vol. XXIV, n. 
68, 1994, p.652. All the more so if it concerns a nullity between Anglicans, who are baptized. 
37 J.Mª. DÍAZ MORENO, Non-canonical marriages and the competence of Ecclesiastical 
Tribunals, in Proceedings of the XXVI Conference of the Spanish Association of Canonists, Madrid, 2006, p. 
89. 
2. A prior undissolved matrimonial bond. 
3. Kinship in the direct line by consanguinity or adoption and collateral 
kinship by consanguinity up to the third degree. 
4. Conviction as perpetrator or accomplice in the death of the spouse of either of 
the new spouses.

Anglican 
Spanish legislation allows marriage to be celebrated and solemnized according 
to the rites and religious requirements of each of the confessions with an Agreement 39. 
Thus, the canonical form 40 and the religious forms agreed in the 
Cooperation Agreements with FEREDE, with the FCI, and with the CIE 41 are admitted. 
There is a peculiarity of the Anglican form of celebration—which affects all 
entities belonging to FEREDE—that stands out when compared with what is 
provided for Jewish and Muslim forms of marriage celebration, namely that 
article 7.1 of the Agreement concluded between the Spanish State and FEREDE says: “The 
civil effects of marriage celebrated before the ministers of worship of the 
Churches belonging to the Federation of Evangelical Religious Entities of Spain are recognized”; 
whereas in article 7.1 of the Agreement concluded with the Jewish Community one reads: 
“The civil effects of marriage celebrated according to the Israelite formal 
regulations before the ministers of worship of the Communities belonging to the 
Federation of Israelite Communities of Spain are recognized”; and in Article 7.1 of the Agreement 
concluded with the Islamic Commission, civil effects are also attributed to those 
marriages celebrated according to the religious form established in Islamic Law. This 
difference in the regulation is due to the fact that, strictly speaking, the members of

FEREDE lack a specific religious form. That said, it should be noted that

each of the aspects to be carried out (and their order) during the

As regards the territorial and personal scope of marriages celebrated in 
Anglican religious form, we wish to highlight that: 
1. Both what is provided in the Cooperation Agreement between the Spanish State and 
FEREDE, and what is provided in the Civil Code, is always applicable if the marriages

Anglican form are foreigners, they are granted the faculty to celebrate the marriage

Spanish law 45.

(CEPPLE).

James I of England and Philip III of Spain, English residents in Spain were authorized to celebrate

participate actively in the life of the Church. 
In the IERE, worship is celebrated according to the ancient Hispanic Liturgy, 
also known as Visigothic or Mozarabic. The so-called Mozarabic, Visigothic, or 
Hispanic rite is the liturgy of the ancient Spanish Church that was consolidated around the 
sixth century on the Iberian Peninsula, in the Visigothic Kingdom of Toledo, and that was practiced in the

Muslim rule) 8. Later it was preserved only in the city of Toledo, under rather

chiefly, of Cardinals Cisneros and Lorenzana. In the mid-nineteenth century the 
IERE, on the initiative of its First Bishop, also began to use for its worship the 
ancient Hispanic liturgy.

essential elements of faith and order for achieving unity among Christians.

contracted within the community of faith, is the physical and spiritual union of a man and 
a woman, with mutual consent and with the intention that it be for life.”

Catholics, if one of them seeks to contract a new marriage with a Catholic party,” in JC, vol. XXIV, n. 
68, 1994, p.652. All the more so if it concerns a nullity between Anglicans, who are baptized.

Tribunals, in Proceedings of the XXVI Conference of the Spanish Association of Canonists, Madrid, 2006, p. 
89. 
2. A prior undissolved matrimonial bond. 
3. Kinship in the direct line by consanguinity or adoption and collateral 
kinship by consanguinity up to the third degree. 
4. Conviction as perpetrator or accomplice in the death of the spouse of either of 
the new spouses.

3.2 Ecclesiastical requirements  
They are the same as those established by the Civil Code and, in addition 38: 
1. It must be verified that the persons have received sufficient instruction to understand the nature, meaning, and purpose of marriage. 
2. It must be verified that at least one of the parties is baptized.

3.3 The form of Anglican celebration 
Spanish legislation allows marriage to be celebrated and solemnized according 
to the rites and religious requirements of each of the confessions with an Agreement 39. 
Thus, the canonical form 40 and the religious forms agreed in the 
Cooperation Agreements with FEREDE, with the FCI, and with the CIE 41 are admitted.

entities belonging to FEREDE—that stands out when compared with what is 
provided for Jewish and Muslim forms of marriage celebration, namely that 
article 7.1 of the Agreement concluded between the Spanish State and FEREDE says: “The 
civil effects of marriage celebrated before the ministers of worship of the 
Churches belonging to the Federation of Evangelical Religious Entities of Spain are recognized”; 
whereas in article 7.1 of the Agreement concluded with the Jewish Community one reads: 
“The civil effects of marriage celebrated according to the Israelite formal 
regulations before the ministers of worship of the Communities belonging to the 
Federation of Israelite Communities of Spain are recognized”; and in Article 7.1 of the Agreement 
concluded with the Islamic Commission, civil effects are also attributed to those 
marriages celebrated according to the religious form established in Islamic Law. This 
difference in the regulation is due to the fact that, strictly speaking, the members of

39 Article 59 establishes that: “Matrimonial consent may be given in the form 
provided by a registered religious confession, on the terms agreed with the State or, failing that, 
authorized by its legislation.” And article 60 completes it by saying that: “Marriage 
celebrated according to the religious forms provided in the preceding article produces civil effects...”.

on December 4, 1979 (published in the BOE of December 15, 1979).

FEREDE lack a specific religious form. That said, it should be noted that 
Anglicans possess a whole ritual of Solemnization of Holy Matrimony, in which 
each of the aspects to be carried out (and their order) during the 
celebration of the marriage ceremony is detailed.

Anglican religious form, we wish to highlight that: 
1. Both what is provided in the Cooperation Agreement between the Spanish State and 
FEREDE, and what is provided in the Civil Code, is always applicable if the marriages 
are celebrated in Spain 42. 
2. It is also possible to request the registration of a marriage celebrated in Anglican religious 
form abroad, if it affects a Spanish citizen 43. 
3. In the event that both spouses of a marriage celebrated in 
Anglican form are foreigners, they are granted the faculty to celebrate the marriage 
in Spain, either according to the personal law 44 of each of them, or according to 
Spanish law 45.

3.4 The marriage file 
Those who wish to contract marriage in Anglican religious form must 
initiate the marriage file before the Judge or Civil Registry officer 
corresponding to the domicile of either of the spouses 46. 
To that end, each of the spouses shall sign a document by which 
the marriage file is opened 47. This document must be accompanied by the evidence

42 Instruction of February 10, 1993 of the Directorate General of Registries and Notaries 
on certain marriages celebrated in religious form (published in the BOE of February 24, 
1993). 
43 Always provided that the validity requirements demanded by Spanish law are respected and that 
the requirements of the legislation in force in the country where the marriage is celebrated are fulfilled. 
44 Art. 9.1 of the Civil Code. 
45 Art. 50 of the Civil Code. 
46 Art. 7.2 of the Cooperation Agreement between the Spanish State and FEREDE and art. 238 of the

47 In this document, according to art. 240 of the Civil Registry Regulations, the personal data of the

spouses. And furthermore: a) if one or both spouses had previously contracted marriage and it had been dissolved,

b) The declaration that there is no impediment to the present marriage. c) The Judge or official chosen, where applicable, for the celebration. In the case

spouses had resided or been domiciled in the last two years. 
of the birth of each of the spouses and of the other particulars that have been 
mentioned 48. 
In the case of marriage celebrated in Anglican religious form, it is also usual 
to provide: the name of the officiating minister of worship; the name and address of the 
Church where the wedding will be celebrated; and the names of the spouses.

validity of six months 50).

prior to the celebration 
Canon 11.2 and 3 requires the officiating Minister of worship, before proceeding to the 
solemnization of a marriage, to verify that 51:

least thirty days before the celebration 52.

content: The Anglican Communion is constituted by the set of Episcopal Churches that belong to the Anglican confession and derives from the extension of the Church of England to other countries. In Spain the Anglican Communion is formed by two episcopal jurisdictions: the Spanish Reformed Episcopal Church 3 (hereinafter, IERE) and the Spanish Section of the Diocese in Europe of the Church of England 4 (also called the Diocese of Gibraltar in Europe). Both jurisdictions are integrated into FEREDE 5.

1 Work published in GARCÍA GARCÍA, R., GONZÁLEZ SÁNCHEZ, M. (Eds.), 
Application and development of the Agreement between the Spanish State and FEREDE, Fundación 
Universitaria Española, Madrid, 2008, pp. 169-188. (ISBN: 978-84-7392-700-0) 
2 I wish to thank D. Carlos López Lozano, Diocesan Bishop of the Spanish Reformed Episcopal Church and Assistant Bishop of the Diocese 
of Gibraltar in Europe, for the help provided in preparing this article. For more information on the subject, see: S. NEILL, Anglicanism, Madrid, 
1986; F. SERRANO ÁLVAREZ, Against Wind and Tide, Terrassa, 2000, and C. LÓPEZ LOZANO, Precedents 
of the I.E.R.E., Madrid, 1991. 
3 It was founded in Gibraltar in 1868 and was reorganized in diocesan form in Seville in 
1880. This foundation arose from a Synod in which the episcopal form of government was adopted. 
It is currently a Member of the Anglican Communion and of the World Council of Churches and belongs to the 
KEK Conference of Churches and to the Conference of Latin Protestant Churches of Southern Europe 
(CEPPLE). 
4 Its origins date from 1605. Thanks to the ratification of the Treaty of London signed by 
James I of England and Philip III of Spain, English residents in Spain were authorized to celebrate 
private worship (in their homes). In 1842 a jurisdiction was created that supervised Anglican chaplaincies 
in Spanish territory, and in 1988 the Diocese in Europe of the Church of 
England was established (to which the Anglican chaplaincies established in Spain belong).  
5 See Structure and composition of the Federation of Evangelical Religious Entities of 
Spain, in Cuadernos de Información, 1-2, 2007, p. 11. 
In Spain, the Anglican Communion has about 39 parishes and chaplaincies, 
with about a hundred places of worship 6 and a membership of about 200,000 people 7 who 
participate actively in the life of the Church. 
In the IERE, worship is celebrated according to the ancient Hispanic Liturgy, 
also known as Visigothic or Mozarabic. The so-called Mozarabic, Visigothic, or 
Hispanic rite is the liturgy of the ancient Spanish Church that was consolidated around the 
sixth century on the Iberian Peninsula, in the Visigothic Kingdom of Toledo, and that was practiced in the 
Hispanic territories until the eleventh century (both in areas under Christian and 
Muslim rule) 8. Later it was preserved only in the city of Toledo, under rather 
precarious conditions. The Mozarabic liturgy has been maintained and celebrated without interruption in Spain 
mainly thanks to the Mozarabic Community of Toledo and the efforts, 
chiefly, of Cardinals Cisneros and Lorenzana. In the mid-nineteenth century the 
IERE, on the initiative of its First Bishop, also began to use for its worship the 
ancient Hispanic liturgy.

2. The concept of marriage in the Anglican Communion 
The life of the Church is governed by the provisions of what is established in the 
Book of Bases and Canons of the IERE 9, which was approved at the XXXVI Synod 10  
and ratified at the XLI Synod 11 and in the spirit of the "Chicago-Lambeth Quadrilateral" 12  
approved by the Lambeth Conference of 1888. This document affirms the 
essential elements of faith and order for achieving unity among Christians. 
Among the canons, canon 11 concerns marriage. It is precisely the one that 
gives us the definition of marriage 13 when it says: “... holy marriage, 
contracted within the community of faith, is the physical and spiritual union of a man and 
a woman, with mutual consent and with the intention that it be for life.”

6 These figures do not coincide with those offered by the Registry of Religious Entities, since 
notification of the opening of a place of worship to the Registry is not obligatory, but optional. 
7 Many of them are retirees from the United Kingdom who have fixed their residence in Spain. This 
explains why the number of marriages celebrated in Anglican form in Spain is not very high, 
since they number around 30 marriages a year. According to data provided by the IERE, in 
2007 it was known that 28 marriages had been celebrated (but as of February 28, 
2008, the statistics were not yet finalized); in 2006, 22 marriages were contracted in Anglican religious form; 
and in 2005, there were 31. 
8 http://www.anglicanos.org/ (consulted March 8, 2007). 
9 Technically they are the Fundamental Bases of denomination, doctrine, personality, government, 
and discipline of the IERE. These Bases were drafted in accordance with the general doctrines of the Anglican Communion 
throughout the world and, once approved, were made known to the Archbishop of 
Canterbury. 
10 It was held on June 10 and 11, 1982. 
11 It was held between June 4 and 6, 1993. 
12 Four things are defined as essential for unity in the Anglican Church, namely: 
a) The Scriptures of the Old and New Testament. 
b) The ecumenical creeds (Apostles' and Nicene). 
c) The Sacraments of Jesus Christ. 
d) The Historic Episcopate. 
13 Canon 11.2.c). 
This definition deserves to be analyzed in detail and, for that reason, we have thought it 
appropriate to dissect it into four parts: 
1st. Holy marriage, contracted within the community of faith. 
Anglicans, members of FEREDE, have the particularity 14 of the 
existence of the Sacraments 15. For them there are two Sacraments: Baptism 16 and the 
Eucharist 17. And five sacramental rites 18: Confirmation 19, Penance 20, 
Marriage, Anointing of the sick 21, and Holy Orders 22. 
Therefore, marriage celebrated in Anglican religious form is a sacramental 
rite. Even 23 when only one of the two spouses is baptized 
Anglican.

14 Like the Roman Catholic Apostolic Church.  
15 Inasmuch as they are actions of Christ and of the Church, they are signs and means by which 
faith is expressed and strengthened, worship is rendered to God, and the sanctification of humankind is carried out, and therefore 
they contribute in great measure to creating, confirming, and manifesting ecclesiastical communion (canon 840 of the 
Code of Canon Law). The Council of Trent solemnly established that there are seven Sacraments 
of the New Law, namely: Baptism, Confirmation, Holy Eucharist, Penance, Extreme Unction, Orders, 
and Marriage. The same enumeration had already been made in the Decree for the Armenians of the Council of 
Florence (1439); in the Profession of Faith of Michael Palaeologus, offered by Gregory X at the Council of 
Lyon (1274); and at the council held in London in 1237. And in the Westminster Confession of Faith, of 
1647, we can read that: "The sacraments ordained by God are not only badges or tokens of the 
Christian man's profession, but rather sure witnesses and effectual signs of grace and of 
God's good will toward us, by which He works invisibly in us and not only 
quickens but also strengthens and confirms our faith in Him" (Chapter XXVII.1). 
16 For Anglicans, Baptism is the doorway into the family of God. It is administered 
once only to each person (generally in childhood). It is performed with water, symbolizing the cleansing of 
sin, and the Most Holy Trinity is invoked. The inward and spiritual gift is union with Christ in his 
death and resurrection, the forgiveness of sins, and a new birth into the family of God: the Church. 
17 It is the commemoration and thanksgiving for the death and resurrection of Christ. 
Bread and wine are used. The body of Christ is given, taken, and eaten in a heavenly and spiritual manner, and 
the means by which it is received and eaten is faith. Through the sacrament of the Eucharist, the members of the 
Church offer themselves to God in repentance, love, and faith, remember his death, testify to his 
sacrifice, and renew their hope in the heavenly meal. The IERE practices a policy of open 
communion toward communicant members of other Christian churches. 
18 The sacramental rites also have sacramental value, since participation in them 
communicates divine grace; but, in the words of Mortimer, “they are not necessary for salvation in the same 
way as the other two sacraments, since they are not necessary for all.” Some also call them 
“the five lesser Sacraments.” 
19 Anglicans understand confirmation as the service by which, through prayer and 
the laying on of hands by the bishop, and with the action of the Holy Spirit, the 
commitment to Christ made in baptism is renewed and strengthened. 
20 Penance is the acknowledgment and confession to God of sins, made freely and 
voluntarily in the presence of a minister, and with a sincere desire to change one's attitude. Through 
absolution, the minister affirms God's forgiveness and the reconciliation of the sinner. 
21 Anointing of the sick is the service by which God's grace is given for physical and spiritual 
healing in response to faith and prayer. It is shown by the laying on of hands or by anointing 
with oil. 
22 Through this rite, Christians are consecrated to the service of God. They receive the power and grace that 
helps them dedicate their lives to the good of the community by teaching, administering the sacraments, and 
governing the Church. 
23 Unlike what is established by Canon Law, which in canon 1055.1 states: “The 
matrimonial covenant… was raised by Christ the Lord to the dignity of a sacrament between the baptized”; and in 
its number 2 establishes: “Therefore, between the baptized, there can be no valid matrimonial contract that is not 
In principle, Anglicans are obliged to celebrate their marriage 
in religious form. Also when only one of the two spouses is 
baptized 24. And, if this situation arises, the unbaptized party is not required to make 
an express declaration committing not to impede the baptized party 
from continuing to participate actively in the life of the Church 25.  
Despite what has been said regarding the obligation to celebrate 
marriage in Anglican religious form, if the spouses decide to marry 
only in civil form, the Church recognizes the existence of that matrimonial bond. 
Moreover, it continues to allow the spouses to participate actively in the life of the 
community. This is probably due to recognition of the human value of their 
civil marriage 26. 
2nd It is the physical 27 and spiritual union of a man and a woman. 
It is a clear expression of the non-acceptance of homosexual marriage, as 
marriage. 
In this sense, the Permanent Commission of FEREDE issued a declaration 
on the effects for the Churches of FEREDE of the modification of the Civil Code in 
matters of marriage 28, which read as follows: 
“After the approval of Law 13/2005 modifying the Civil Code in 
matters of marriage, the Plenary Commission after due deliberation 
agrees: 
a. To ratify that, in marriage celebrated according to the evangelical rite, under 
the Cooperation Agreements, the spouses must be a man and a woman. 
b. That certifications for the celebration of marriages by the 
evangelical rite shall not be issued when the spouses are persons of the same sex.

be a sacrament.” Thus, marriage between two baptized persons, if it is a valid marriage, is always 
a sacrament. And if one of the spouses is unbaptized, it cannot be a sacramental marriage.  
24 Canon 11.2.d). 
25 This practice stands out as different from that of the Roman Catholic Apostolic Church, which 
establishes in its canon 1125, 1º and 2º: “If there is a just and reasonable cause, the local Ordinary may 
grant this permission; but he must not grant it unless the following conditions are fulfilled: 1º that the 
Catholic party declare that they are prepared to remove dangers of defecting from the faith, and sincerely promise 
to do all in their power to have all the offspring baptized and brought up in the Catholic 
Church; 2º that the other party be informed at an appropriate time of the promises which the Catholic party 
is to make, so that it is certain that the non-Catholic party is truly aware of the promise and of the obligation of the 
Catholic party.” 
26 In this sense, see M.F. POMPEDDA, Fede e Sacramento del matrimonio. Mancanza di 
Fede e consenso matrimoniale: aspetti giuridici, in Quaderni, Studio Rotale, II, Rome, 1987, pp. 41-71. 
27 Procreation is not one of the essential purposes of marriage. Sexuality is 
understood as a gift of God. This contrasts with what is established in canon 1055.1 of the Code of 
Canon Law: “The matrimonial covenant, by which a man and a woman establish between themselves a 
partnership of the whole of life, is by its nature ordered toward the good of the spouses and the 
procreation and education of offspring…”; and in canon 1096.1: “For matrimonial consent 
to exist, it is necessary that the contracting parties at least not be ignorant that marriage is a permanent 
partnership between a man and a woman ordered to the procreation of offspring…”. 
28 This declaration arose from the meeting of the Permanent Commission of FEREDE held on 
October 11, 2005. 
c. That ministers of worship who, in fulfillment of what is set out above, 
intend to celebrate or do celebrate marriages between two persons of the same 
sex, by the evangelical rite and under the Cooperation Agreements, shall be 
automatically deprived of the conformity of the Permanent Commission of 
FEREDE. Therefore, as established by article 3 of Law 24/1992, they cease to be 
considered ministers of worship for the purposes of the said law. 
d. That Churches or ministers of worship who breach these agreements shall be 
subject to proceedings that will be referred to the Plenary Commission or 
Permanent Commission so that they may decide what they consider appropriate.” 
From this we can note that: 
1. At the time of the approval of the Cooperation Agreement concluded between the 
Spanish State and FEREDE 29, the provisions of article 7 were 
conceived only for marriages celebrated between a man and a woman 
(for that was also the only option for marriage contracted in civil form). By 
contrast, today, even though it is possible to contract civil marriage between two 
persons of the same sex, the Churches belonging to FEREDE indicate 
expressly that for marriages celebrated in their religious form, the 
requirement that the spouses be of different sex continues to apply. 
2. This interpretation is possible because of the separation existing between the Spanish 
State and the various religious confessions. Hence the modification made in the 
Civil Code affects only civil marriages, insofar as the religious 
confessions position themselves against the adoption of these postulates. 
3rd. With mutual consent. 
This means that the parties must have sufficient capacity to understand what 
marriage is 30, and that consent must be manifested in a 
completely free manner 31. 
4th. With the intention that it be for life. 
This means that marriage is conceived as indissoluble, and to that end, 
Anglicans have, in principle, no mechanism for dissolving the matrimonial bond. 
Nevertheless, this statement must be qualified on the basis of: 
a) A civil avenue: the effect of civil divorce is recognized. Although divorce 32 
is considered a grave error in Anglican practice and “a priori” the divorced are not permitted 
to contract a new marriage 33.

29 By Law 24/1992, of November 10 (published in the BOE of November 12, 
1992).  
30 Canon 11.2.c). 
31 This freedom must be both internal and external. That is, there can be no conditioning 
of any kind at the moment of the external manifestation of consent. Precisely at this 
point we see the concordance between what is required by Canon Law—which in its canon 1103 says: “Marriage

This is logical, since the freedom with which marriage must be contracted is a requirement of

b) An ecclesiastical avenue: following what is provided in Doctrinal Base Six 34, the

could pronounce itself regarding the dissolution of a flagrant case of failure of a 
marriage. 
And there would even be a third avenue (also ecclesiastical) corresponding to the 
Roman Catholic Apostolic Church: those cases in which a 
non-Catholic party seeks to challenge their marriage before an ecclesiastical judge—even 
while the challenging party remains non-Catholic—in order to contract a canonical marriage 
with a Catholic person 36. It would even be possible that the canonical legislator had 
taken into account the fact that many Christian Churches and communities lack 
a proper matrimonial judicial system and, therefore, no foreign territory would be being invaded 37.

form

For a marriage contracted in Anglican religious form to have civil 
validity, it is required: a) that there be true matrimonial consent; and b) that there be no 
legal impediments. 
a) True matrimonial consent. 
Article 45 of the Civil Code states: “There is no marriage without matrimonial 
consent. Any condition, term, or mode of the consent shall be deemed not 
written.” 
b) That there be no legal impediments. 
These are those established in articles 46 and 47 of the Civil Code: 
1. Minority of age without emancipation.

32 Divorce does not cause one to fall into excommunication. 
33 To avoid falling into the same error again. But, extraordinarily, a new marriage is permitted 
provided that the divorced person interested in remarrying 
had not been the cause of the divorce for reasons of adultery or infidelity, unless they demonstrate 
that they have resolved the problem that caused their first marital failure. 
34 Chapter II of the Bases, dedicated to the general organization of the Church. 
35 It is subject to the authority of Christ.

marriage are: 1º the spouses…”; canon 1476: “Any person, whether baptized or not, may sue

89.

3. Kinship in the direct line by consanguinity or adoption and collateral 
kinship by consanguinity up to the third degree. 
4. Conviction as perpetrator or accomplice in the death of the spouse of either of 
the new spouses.

They are the same as those established by the Civil Code and, in addition 38: 
1. It must be verified that the persons have received sufficient instruction to understand the nature, meaning, and purpose of marriage. 
2. It must be verified that at least one of the parties is baptized.

form abroad, if it affects a Spanish citizen 43. 
3. In the event that both spouses of a marriage celebrated in 
Anglican form are foreigners, they are granted the faculty to celebrate the marriage 
in Spain, either according to the personal law 44 of each of them, or according to 
Spanish law 45.

3.4 The marriage file 
Those who wish to contract marriage in Anglican religious form must 
initiate the marriage file before the Judge or Civil Registry officer 
corresponding to the domicile of either of the spouses 46. 
To that end, each of the spouses shall sign a document by which 
the marriage file is opened 47. This document must be accompanied by the evidence

42 Instruction of February 10, 1993 of the Directorate General of Registries and Notaries 
on certain marriages celebrated in religious form (published in the BOE of February 24, 
1993). 
43 Always provided that the validity requirements demanded by Spanish law are respected and that 
the requirements of the legislation in force in the country where the marriage is celebrated are fulfilled. 
44 Art. 9.1 of the Civil Code. 
45 Art. 50 of the Civil Code. 
46 Art. 7.2 of the Cooperation Agreement between the Spanish State and FEREDE and art. 238 of the 
Civil Registry Regulations. 
47 In this document, according to art. 240 of the Civil Registry Regulations, the personal data of the 
spouses shall be indicated: the identity particulars and even the profession of the 
spouses. And furthermore: a) if one or both spouses had previously contracted marriage and it had been dissolved, 
the name and surnames of the previous spouse or spouses and the date of the dissolution of the marriage. 
b) The declaration that there is no impediment to the present marriage. c) The Judge or official chosen, where applicable, for the celebration. In the case 
that concerns us, this would be the officiating minister of worship. d) The list of the towns in which the 
spouses had resided or been domiciled in the last two years. 
of the birth of each of the spouses and of the other particulars that have been 
mentioned 48. 
In the case of marriage celebrated in Anglican religious form, it is also usual 
to provide: the name of the officiating minister of worship; the name and address of the 
Church where the wedding will be celebrated; and the names of the spouses.  
When the Civil Registry officer has accredited the matrimonial capacity 
of the spouses, he issues a certificate of matrimonial capacity 49 (which has a 
validity of six months 50).

3.5 Requirements of the Anglican Communion prior to the celebration 
Canon 11.2 and 3 requires the officiating Minister of worship, before proceeding to the 
solemnization of a marriage, to verify that 51: 
a) Both parties have received instruction concerning the nature, 
meaning, and purpose of marriage. 
b) Both parties understand that marriage is the physical and spiritual union of 
a man and a woman, with mutual consent and with the intention that it be for 
life. 
c) At least one of the parties has been baptized. 
d) Notification of the parties' intention to marry must have been given, at 
least thirty days before the celebration 52. 
e) The corresponding banns have been published (once only), during 
the celebration of the Divine Office of the Sunday preceding the day on which the 
marriage is to be solemnized, in the form prescribed in the Liturgy.

48 Habitually this consists of the literal certificate of the birth registration; the 
original and photocopy of the D.N.I. (or N.I.E.); the certificate (or certificates) of registration or of the place 
of residence for the last two years; and the declaration of two witnesses (provided with their D.N.I.). 
49 Art. 7.3 of the Agreement between the Spanish State and FEREDE. The model certificate of 
matrimonial capacity was approved by an Order of January 21, 1993 (published in the BOE 
of February 3, 1993). 
50 Art. 7.4 of the Agreement. 
51 In canon 11, in addition to the requirements we set out, it is also indicated that the Minister may not 
solemnize any marriage without having verified that “the spouses have already celebrated the 
matrimonial contract before the competent civil authority.” It must be understood that, tacitly, this 
prescription is repealed, inasmuch as it only made sense before the approval of the corresponding 
Cooperation Agreement with FEREDE. 
52 Unless, for a very justified cause, the Minister agrees to dispense with this requirement, if one 
of the parties is a communicant member of his Congregation, or if he can provide satisfactory proof of 
his responsibility. In that case, the Minister shall inform—in writing—the Diocesan Bishop 
immediately. 
3.6 Celebration and subsequent registration in the Civil Registry 
At the time of the celebration there must be present, at least, two 
witnesses, who shall sign—together with the spouses and the celebrating Minister—
the record that will be delivered to the Civil Registry in order to proceed with the registration of the 
marriage 53. 
As regards standing to register a marriage celebrated in 
Anglican religious form, according to canon 11 54, it is the officiating Minister of worship who 
shall enter in the corresponding Register: the date and place of the solemnization of the 
marriage; the names of the contracting parties and the names of their parents; the age 
of the spouses; their domiciles; the numbers of their identity documents; their 
religious condition; the names, domiciles, identity documents, and religious 
condition of the witnesses. 
Nevertheless, since article 7 of the 1992 Agreement does not expressly establish 
who holds this standing 55, we think that the spouses, the officiating minister, 
and even a third party with an interest in it (normally a relative or a 
friend of the spouses) have it. Subsequently, by Order of the Ministry of 
Justice of January 21, 1993, it is established that completion of the certificate of 
matrimonial celebration corresponds to the representative of the religious Entity 56. It seems 
that with this provision the aim is to guarantee that the officiant is truly one of the 
ministers of worship of the religious Entity in question. 
There is no established time limit for registration 57. In this way, late 
registration is made possible 58, and certain problems can arise, for example: that a 
marriage has been celebrated in Anglican religious form and has not been 
registered in the Civil Registry and, once six months have elapsed since the 
issuance of the certificate of matrimonial capacity, a new 
file is promoted, a new certificate of capacity is obtained, and a second 
marriage is contracted. This is perfectly possible, since neither a civil sanction nor 
a criminal sanction is provided for the case in which neither the spouses nor the celebrating Minister of worship 
proceed to register in the Civil Registry the marriage celebrated. 
It is also worth noting that, although for the recognition of civil 
effects of marriage celebrated in Anglican religious form the 
registration of that marriage in the Civil Registry is necessary 59, once that 
registration takes place—even if late—the effects always relate back to the moment of the 
celebration. This must be the only viable interpretation, since the Civil Registry Law 
establishes 60: “The civil effects of canonical or civil marriage shall be produced 
from the celebration. For the effects to be recognized, the registration of the

54 Number 3, section d).

56 This regulation is common to FEREDE, the FCI, and the CIE.

marriage.” Of course, this same regime will be the one applied to the rest of 
marriages celebrated in religious form by the confessions with an Agreement. 
We must even note that the Constitutional Court goes further when 
it states that, even though a marriage celebrated in religious form 61 is not 
registered, in the event of the death of one of the two spouses, the surviving spouse has 
the right to a widow's or widower's pension, for although the unregistered marriage lacks 
full civil effects, it does give rise to certain effects. And one of those effects is, 
precisely, Social Security protection 62. 
4. Conclusions 
When we speak of marriage celebrated in Anglican religious form we refer 
rather to a liturgical specificity than to a proper Anglican matrimonial 
law, inasmuch as—like the other Churches that arose after the Reformation—what is 
sought is to set aside what is strictly juridical in order to give greater importance to the 
pastoral. Proof of this is the recognition among Anglican faithful of a marriage 
celebrated in civil form.  
For Anglicans, marriage is considered a natural institution, a 
sacred institution 63, and an institution that at the same time participates in a secular nature 
(inasmuch as its regulation and the regulation of its dissolution correspond to the civil 
legislator). 
It is true that celebration in religious form involves a presentation of the 
sacramental rite before the Church itself for the reception of the nuptial blessing. 
As we have seen, divorce is admitted—even though it is considered a 
grave error—and the Anglican Communion does not have a jurisdiction of its own to hear 
matrimonial disputes (which, therefore, will remain reserved for the civil 
jurisdiction).

61 Always provided that it is the marriage proper to one of the confessions with an Agreement. 
62 STC 199/2004, of November 15. See also the following doctrinal study: I. 
ALDANONDO, Effects of unregistered canonical marriage in the area of widow's pensions, in 
Iustel, RGDCDEE, n. 15, October 2007. 
63 Not sacramental (although it is a sacramental rite). 
1. No Minister shall solemnize without written permission of his Bishop the marriage of 
persons who have not previously celebrated the matrimonial contract before the 
competent civil authority 64. 
2. On the Sunday preceding the day on which the marriage is to be solemnized, the Minister 
shall publish once only (during the Divine Office) the Banns, in this manner:  
    “I publish the Banns of Marriage between M... M... and N... N... If any of 
you know cause or just impediment why these persons may not be 
joined in holy matrimony, you are bound in conscience to declare it.” 
3. On the day and hour appointed for solemnizing the marriage, the spouses shall come 
to the Church with their relatives and friends, and approaching the Sanctuary, the 
woman standing on the left side of the man, the Minister shall begin saying:    
“In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. R [Response]. Amen. V 
[Versicle]. Behold, God is our helper. R. The Lord is with those who uphold our 
life. V. O God, save us by your name. R. And defend us with your power. V. 
Help us, O God, our salvation, who uphold our life, that we may 
rejoice in your holy name; and grant that all who are called by the name of Christ 
may enjoy spiritual union with him, and thus may bear present 
adversities and obtain eternal joys, that we may praise you for all and 
rejoice that you are in us and we in you. R. Amen. V. Through your 
mercy, O our God, who are blessed and live and govern all things forever 
and ever. R. Amen. 
4. Then the Minister shall speak to the spouses, saying:  
 DOES each of you desire, and are you willing, to confirm and sanctify before 
God and in the presence of this congregation, the bond of holy matrimony? 
Each of the spouses shall answer: “This I desire and to this I am willing with the 
grace of God.” 
Minister: “I require and charge you, that if either of you knows any 
impediment why you may not be lawfully married in the Church of Christ, you 
declare it. For you must be certain that those who join otherwise than 
as the Word of God provides and approves are not joined in God, nor is their marriage 
lawful in the Church.” 
5. If no impediment appears, let this Antiphon be sung or read:  
“Marriage is honorable in all. And the marriage bed undefiled. This is a great mystery, 
in Christ and in the Church. Glory and honor to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, 
forever and ever. Amen.” 
6. After the Antiphon, the Congregation kneeling, the Minister standing, let him continue:

64 It must be understood that this is repealed, inasmuch as this provision is prior to the entry into force 
of the Cooperation Agreements of 1992. 
    “The Lord be always with you. R. And with your spirit. V. Let us pray to God our 
heavenly Father and with all supplication beseech him that he would graciously deign to bless 
these two children of his, with the grace of his Christ our Lord and with the virtue of the Holy 
Spirit. R. Grant us this, eternal and almighty God.” 
 7. All:   
    “Our Father, who art in heaven: Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. 
Thy will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily 
bread. And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our 
debtors. And lead us not into temptation. But deliver us from evil. Amen.” 
8. The Minister:  
   “Deliver us from evil, and confirm us in your fear with every good work, O God and our Lord. 
Hear our petitions, and grant that these two servants of yours may be 
prepared with your grace to enter the holy estate of marriage. Through our 
Lord Jesus Christ your Son, who with you lives and reigns in the unity of the Holy Spirit, one 
God, forever and ever. R. Amen.” 
9. The Congregation seated, the Minister may read what follows:  
    “All who are married and those who intend to enter the married 
estate, listen carefully to what the Holy Scriptures say concerning the duty 
that husbands have toward their wives. The apostle Paul, in his epistle to the 
Ephesians, says: “Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the Church, and gave 
himself for it, that he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the 
word, that he might present it to himself a glorious Church, not having spot, or 
wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish. So ought men 
to love their wives as their own bodies. He that loveth his wife loveth himself. 
For no man ever yet hated his own flesh; but nourisheth and cherisheth it, 
even as the Lord the Church. For we are members of his body, of his flesh, and 
of his bones. For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined unto his 
wife, and they two shall be one flesh. This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning 
Christ and the Church. Nevertheless let every one of you in particular so love his wife 
even as himself.”  
And the apostle Peter, in his First Epistle, also says to married men: 
    “Husbands, dwell with them according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife, as unto the weaker 
vessel, and as being heirs together of the grace of life, that your prayers be not 
hindered.

Hear now, you wives, and learn what your duty is toward your 
husbands, according to the same Word of God.” Paul says in the aforementioned Epistle to the 
Ephesians: “Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as unto the Lord. For the 
husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the head of the Church; and he is the saviour of the body. 
Therefore as the Church is subject unto Christ, so let the wives 
be to their own husbands in every thing.” And Peter, in his aforementioned First Epistle, says: 
“Wives, be in subjection to your own husbands; that, if any obey not the Word, 
they also may without the Word be won by the conversation of the wives; while they behold your chaste 
conversation coupled with fear. Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of 
plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel; but let it be the hidden man 
of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, 
which is in the sight of God of great price. For after this manner in the old time the holy women also, 
who trusted in God, adorned themselves, being in subjection unto their own 
husbands: even as Sara obeyed Abraham, calling him lord: whose daughters ye are, 
as long as ye do well, and are not afraid with any amazement.” 
10. After this reading, or in place of it, the Minister may, if he thinks it 
fitting, declare in brief words to the spouses:  
[What the institution, use, and ends of marriage are, and the duties of each of the 
spouses toward the other]. 
[Exhorting them to study the Word of God, that they may learn to live by faith and be 
content amid cares and labors]. 
[Praying much together, and one for the other, mutually stimulating one another to good 
works and living as befits heirs of eternal life]. 
11. The address concluded, and the Congregation kneeling, let the Minister pray 
saying: “Eternal God, Creator and Preserver of humankind, Giver of all 
spiritual grace and Author of everlasting life! Since your presence and favor are happiness 
in every condition and sweeten all our relations, we ask you in the name of 
Christ, that as You have brought these your servants together in your providence, you would sanctify them 
with your divine Spirit, preparing and disposing their hearts for the estate of 
marriage, and enriching them with every kind of grace, that, as befits 
Christians, they may fulfill the duties, enjoy the consolations, bear the burdens, and 
resist the temptations that accompany that estate, and continuing always together 
in peace and affection, live according to your holy commandments. Through Jesus Christ 
our Lord. R. Amen.” 
12. The Congregation seated, and the spouses standing, let the Minister say to the man:   
 “Take the hand of your wife, and repeat after me”: 
Let the man take the woman's right hand, and say following the Minister:  
    “I, M... M..., declare before God and in the presence of his Church, that I receive you, 
N... N..., as my lawful wife, and I promise to be to you a loving and faithful husband, until 
God is pleased to separate us by death.” 
13. Then let the Minister say to the woman:  
 “Now take you the hand of your husband and repeat after me”: 
Let the woman take the man's right hand and say following the Minister:  
    “I, N.... N..., certify before God and in the presence of his Church, that I receive 
you, M... M..., as my lawful husband, and I promise to be to you a loving, obedient, 
and faithful wife, until God is pleased to separate us by death.” 
14. Then let the Minister give the man the wedding Ring, that he may place it on the 
ring finger of the woman's left hand, and holding the ring there, let the man say:  
    “Receive this ring, as earnest and pledge of the fulfillment of my promise and as 
a symbol of our holy union” 65. 
15. The man and the woman shall kneel, and the Minister, joining their right hands, 
shall say:  
“Those whom God has joined together, let no one put asunder.” 
16. And addressing the Congregation, let him add:  
 “Forasmuch as M... M... and N... N... have certified their holy marriage, testifying it 
before God and in the presence of his Church, I recognize and declare them to be 
husband and wife, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.”

17. Afterwards he gives the blessing to the spouses, saying: “God the Father, God the Son, 
God the Holy Spirit, bless, preserve, and keep you. R. Amen. V. The Lord by his 
mercy turn toward you the eyes of his favor. R. Amen. V. And so fill you 
with his graces and spiritual blessings, that after having lived in this 
world, together in his fear, you may at last enjoy in the other the eternal life. R. Amen.”  
18. All standing, one of Psalms 127 and 128 may be sung or read, at the Minister's choice.  
19. Then, the Congregation kneeling, the Minister standing shall say: “V. O Lord, save 
your servant and your handmaid. R. Who put their trust in you. V. O Lord, send them help 
from your sanctuary. R. And defend them forever. V. Be you their tower and fortress. R. Before 
their enemies. V. Hear, O Lord, our prayer. R. And let our cry come unto you. V. O 
God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Jacob! Bless these your servants, and sow the seed 
of eternal life in their hearts, that they may put into practice all that they learn 
in your holy Word. Look upon them graciously from heaven, and as in former times 
you granted Abraham and Sarah your favor for their great comfort, deign to extend it 
also upon these your servants, that obeying your will and living securely 
under your protection, they may continue in your holy love until the end of their life. Through 
Jesus Christ our Lord. R. Amen.” 
20. The Deacon: “Brothers and sisters, bow for the blessing.” 
21. The Minister: “The Lord be always with you. R. And with your spirit. V. 
May almighty God bless us with his heavenly goods, and fill us with his spiritual 
gifts. R. Amen. V. Grant us charity, joy, patience, meekness, hope, faith, 
and purity. R. Amen. V. That filled with all his goods we may arrive at the life of

65 If the spouses so request, the arras (wedding coins) will be exchanged at this moment. 
eternal blessedness. R. Amen. V. Through the mercy of the same our God, who 
is blessed and lives and governs all things forever and ever. R. Amen.” 
22. A Hymn may be sung. 
23. And then the Minister dismisses the Congregation, saying: “The peace of God, which 
surpasses all understanding, keep your hearts and your minds in 
Christ Jesus. Amen.” 
24. The spouses and the witnesses shall provide the data necessary for the Minister 
to enter the Marriage Certificate in the corresponding register book.  
25. It is fitting that the spouses receive Holy Communion at the first 
opportunity after their wedding.
